chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## A Company at an Inflection

Two decisions in quick succession redrew Harmonic's strategic map. In February 2024, Nimrod Ben-Natan — who had spent more than two decades inside the company since the 1999 DiviCom acquisition and most recently served as senior vice president and general manager of the Cable Edge business — took the president and chief executive officer title at Harmonic Inc. (HLIT, NASDAQ), succeeding Walter Jankovic, who had held the post on an interim basis following Patrick Harshman's September 2023 retirement. Harshman had led the company for twenty-six years; Jankovic returned to his chief financial officer role under Ben-Natan. Simultaneously, Harmonic accelerated a formal review of its Video segment, eventually announcing its outright sale to MediaKind. Together, the leadership change and the Video divestiture aimed to refocus a San Jose, California company — founded in 1988 — onto a single strategic proposition: that the cable industry's multi-year shift to Unified DOCSIS 4.0 would sustain and accelerate demand for Harmonic's virtualised cable access software.

## Two Segments, One Direction

Harmonic reported two segments. The **Broadband segment** comprised cOS™, a virtualised cable modem termination system (vCMTS) running on commercial off-the-shelf servers, together with complementary distributed-access-architecture hardware — including virtual Broadband Network Gateway, Jetty Remote Switch, and Ripple DAA node — and cloud orchestration tooling. The **Video segment** provided software-based video processing and delivery for broadcasters and media operators. As of the 23 May 2026 frozen snapshot, the Video segment was in the terminal stage of a $145 million all-cash sale to MediaKind (Leone Media Inc.), announced on 8 December 2025 and formalised via an Asset Purchase Agreement executed 20 March 2026 following French employee works council consultation. Closing was expected in the second quarter of 2026. [Source](https://www.harmonicinc.com/press-releases/harmonic-announces-pending-sale-of-its-video-business-to-mediakind)

Ben-Natan framed the rationale in one sentence: the transaction would "advance the growth strategies of both companies," leaving a post-separation Harmonic as a pure-play broadband access platform vendor.

## Revenue Arc and the DOCSIS Transition Trough

Harmonic's consolidated revenues rose from $377 million in 2020 to a record $679 million in FY2024, with the Broadband segment contributing $488 million and the Video segment $191 million. [(SEC EDGAR, CIK 0000851310)](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310)

| Fiscal Year | Total Revenue ($M) | Broadband ($M) | Video ($M) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 646 | — | — |
| 2023 | 610 | — | — |
| 2024 | 679 | 488 | 191 |
| 2025 | 571 | 361 | ~210 |
| 2026F | — | 475–495 | divesting |

FY2025 consolidated revenue fell to $570.8 million as the cable industry's pause ahead of Unified DOCSIS 4.0 commercial deployment compressed near-term Broadband volumes. Ben-Natan had pre-signalled the move at the FY2024 earnings call:

> "We're navigating a shift to Unified DOCSIS 4.0 in 2025, which will result in below-trend revenue due to timing, but we're maintaining our technology and market share leadership. We expect strong cash flow in 2025 and are positioned for above-market trend growth in 2026."

The recovery arrived on schedule. Q4 2025 Broadband bookings reached a record $346.9 million in a single quarter — a 3.5 book-to-bill ratio — lifting total backlog and deferred revenue to $573.8 million, up 73 percent year-over-year. [(Harmonic Q4 2025 press release)](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/HLIT/harmonic-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-ksniufy4i1ch.html) In Q1 2026, Broadband revenue rose 43 percent year-over-year to $121.7 million; management raised full-year 2026 Broadband guidance to $475–$495 million. [(Harmonic Q1 2026 press release)](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/HLIT/harmonic-announces-first-quarter-2026-p6n817lbqhe3.html)

## The Comcast Anchor

Harmonic's CableOS deployment at Comcast began in 2018 and remained the franchise's commercial cornerstone. By the third quarter of 2025 Comcast accounted for 43 percent of Harmonic's consolidated revenue. The operator was adding roughly one million new fibre passings per year using Harmonic's converged cOS platform — spanning residential, commercial, and BEAD-funded rural programmes — with 1.2 million additional locations targeted by end-2025. [(Harmonic-Comcast announcement)](https://www.harmonicinc.com/press-releases/harmonic-and-comcast-work-together-to-expand-fiber-broadband-access) Across the broader industry, cOS was deployed at 127 operators serving 33.3 million cable modems at end-2024, with ten Tier 1 operators engaged on Unified DOCSIS 4.0 trials or early commercial programmes. At the Q3 2025 earnings call, Ben-Natan set out the competitive framing:

> "At this scale, the gap between Harmonic and the rest of the market has become extraordinary. Our field-proven consistency, operational depth, and nearly decade-long production maturity place our platform in a class of its own."

## Dossier Questions

Four structural questions drive the analysis that follows. Whether Comcast's roughly one-million-passings-per-year deployment rate proves durable as the operator manages its own capital envelope and competitive pressures. Whether Unified DOCSIS 4.0 adoption accelerates across the broader North American and international cable operator base in line with the record $582 million backlog Harmonic carried into Q1 2026. Whether the MediaKind transaction closes on schedule and delivers the full $145 million in cash — resolving eighteen months of strategic ambiguity around the Video segment. And how Harmonic defends its virtualised access platform against Cisco Systems, CommScope, Vecima Networks, and the Arista Networks adjacency entrants that have begun circling the cable access software layer.

---

chapters.title: From 1988 founding through DiviCom, Comcast CableOS, Harshman, Ben-Natan
chapters.body:
## Origins in Digital Video

Harmonic was incorporated in San Jose, California, in 1988 as a developer of fibre-optic transmission technology for cable television headend facilities. The founding thesis was precise: the analogue cable plant lacked the bandwidth and modulation efficiency to carry digital video services that operators and broadcasters were beginning to design, and the engineering gap required specialist hardware that the incumbent telecommunications vendors were not positioned to supply. The founding engineers built digital video encoding and compression systems at a moment when the commercial infrastructure for broadcast-quality digital distribution barely existed outside the laboratory.

The company listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker HLIT in 1995, raising capital that extended its sales reach into North American cable headends and European broadcast facilities. The mid-1990s were a period of rapid growth for the digital video encoding market: satellite operators were launching digital services aggressively, European regulators were mandating digital television switchovers, and North American cable operators were beginning the analogue-to-digital migration that would take the better part of a decade to complete. Harmonic was among the few specialist vendors with the engineering depth to supply multiplexers, encoders, and modulation equipment at the scale those rollouts required.

## The DiviCom Acquisition

The transaction that most durably shaped the subsequent three decades of Harmonic's trajectory was the acquisition of DiviCom in 1999. DiviCom was an Israeli developer of digital video encoding and conditional access systems; Nimrod Ben-Natan, who would become Harmonic's chief executive twenty-five years later, was among its co-founders and senior executives. The deal was valued at approximately $780 million in Harmonic stock at announcement, one of the larger Israeli technology acquisitions of the first dot-com cycle, and it substantially expanded Harmonic's engineering depth in MPEG compression standards and digital video systems integration.

Ben-Natan joined Harmonic through the DiviCom transaction and remained with the combined company across successive senior roles over the following two and a half decades. His retention through multiple strategic pivots — from hardware-centric broadcast encoding through software-defined video processing and eventually to the virtualised cable access platform that became CableOS — gave him an unusually complete view of the company's technical heritage, product architecture, and customer relationships.

Patrick Harshman, who had assumed the chief executive role in 1997, oversaw the DiviCom integration and continued to lead the company through the subsequent cycles of the broadcast and cable equipment market. His twenty-six-year tenure made him one of the longer-serving chief executives among listed North American technology equipment companies.

## Building CableOS

The strategic inflection that would come to define Harmonic's positioning in the 2020s was initiated in the middle of the previous decade. Around 2016, Harshman's engineering organisation began development of what would become CableOS: a software-defined, cloud-native virtualisation of the cable modem termination system — the CMTS — that had historically been delivered as purpose-built proprietary hardware installed in cable operator headend facilities. The engineering thesis was technically radical for a market accustomed to multi-year hardware refresh cycles. A virtualised CMTS running on commodity off-the-shelf server infrastructure could, in principle, allow a cable operator to expand broadband capacity through software configuration rather than the laborious physical installation of proprietary chassis across thousands of headend sites.

The development period from 2016 to 2018 required close collaboration with a customer willing to commit engineering resources to a platform without commercial precedent. Comcast Corporation, the largest United States cable operator by subscriber count, became that anchor partner. The first Comcast CableOS deployment went live in 2018, representing the commercial validation of the virtualised CMTS model at an operator of genuine national scale. The deployment marked Harmonic's transition from a video equipment manufacturer with a cable customer base into something categorically different: a software platform company with the largest cable operator in the country as its principal scaling partner.

Revenue data filed with the [Securities and Exchange Commission (CIK 0000851310)](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310) shows the commercial impact of the subsequent deployment scaling:

| Fiscal Year | Total Revenue (USD millions) |
|---|---|
| 2019 | $384 |
| 2020 | $377 |
| 2021 | $499 |
| 2022 | $646 |
| 2023 | $610 |
| 2024 | $580 |

The acceleration from $377 million in 2020 to $646 million in 2022 tracked the broadening of Comcast's CableOS rollout as the operator moved beyond early-trial configurations toward full network deployment. By 2022 the Broadband segment, anchored by CableOS at Comcast, had become the company's dominant revenue contributor. Charter Communications and a broader base of domestic and international cable operators were added as customers, extending the platform's commercial reach beyond the anchor deployment.

## Gallagher, Governance, and the Harshman Retirement

Patrick Gallagher, a former senior executive at Sprint Corporation with deep telecommunications industry operating experience, joined the Harmonic board and assumed the chairmanship in 2022. His arrival preceded by roughly a year the leadership transition that would reshape the company's executive structure.

Patrick Harshman announced his retirement as president and chief executive officer in September 2023, ending a twenty-six-year tenure that had carried Harmonic through the analogue-to-digital encoding transition of the late 1990s, the DiviCom integration, the video-over-IP pivot of the 2000s and 2010s, and the foundational years of the CableOS programme at Comcast. He did not depart the company entirely; Harshman remained on the board of directors following his retirement, preserving continuity of institutional memory at the governance level through the succession period that followed.

Walter Jankovic, who had served as chief financial officer, assumed the interim chief executive role immediately following Harshman's departure. The interim period extended across several months as the board conducted its succession process. Jankovic subsequently returned to the CFO function when the permanent appointment was completed.

## Ben-Natan's Succession

In February 2024, [Harmonic named Nimrod Ben-Natan](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) as president and chief executive officer. The appointment brought to the chief executive role a technologist who had joined the company through the DiviCom acquisition a quarter-century earlier and had spent the intervening years in senior product and operating positions, most recently as senior vice president and general manager of the Cable Edge business — the internal organisation that had built and commercialised CableOS through the Comcast deployment and the broader cable operator scaling.

Ben-Natan's succession was structured as a product-line-native appointment at the precise inflection point when the cable industry was entering the multi-year DOCSIS 4.0 technology upgrade cycle. DOCSIS 4.0 — the next-generation cable modem standard supporting multi-gigabit symmetrical throughput — required cable operators to upgrade their access infrastructure, and CableOS was positioned as the software-defined vehicle through which operators could execute that upgrade without reverting to proprietary hardware procurement cycles. Ben-Natan characterised the deployment opportunity in his early public statements as a long-duration structural demand driver rather than a short-cycle product refresh, emphasising the breadth of the operator upgrade programme still ahead.

Bart Spriester assumed the senior vice president and general manager role for the Cable Access product line organisation following Ben-Natan's elevation, providing operational continuity within the CableOS commercial programme. Jay Stein continued as chief technology officer across the Broadband and Video segments.

## The Video Separation

Alongside the CEO succession, Harmonic announced in 2024 its intention to separate the Video segment as a standalone business. The Video segment — encompassing the company's software-based video processing and delivery solutions for media customers, the direct lineage of the 1988 founding business and the DiviCom acquisition — had operated alongside the Broadband segment for the entirety of Harmonic's history as a listed company.

The separation announcement reflected a strategic posture refinement that the revenue trajectory had made increasingly legible. The Broadband segment's growth through the Comcast CableOS deployment had progressively increased its share of consolidated revenue, while the Video segment faced the structural headwinds of a broadcast equipment market in secular transition as media companies shifted production and distribution workflows to cloud-native platforms. Robert Folliard, senior vice president of the Video division, led the separation planning process under Ben-Natan's direction.

The post-separation entity — the Broadband-focused Harmonic — would be more narrowly concentrated on the CableOS platform, the DOCSIS 4.0 deployment cycle, and the cable operator customer base anchored by Comcast. The Video separation, combined with the Ben-Natan succession, completed a repositioning that had been building since the 2018 Comcast deployment: from a dual-segment broadcast and cable equipment vendor into a focused virtualised cable access platform company at the centre of the cable industry's largest infrastructure transition in a generation.

chapters.title: Broadband (CableOS), Video segment being separated, and DOCSIS 4.0 context
chapters.body:
## The Architecture Shift: Software Replaces Silicon

For most of the cable industry's modern history, the cable modem termination system — the CMTS, the piece of electronics that sits at the headend and manages data traffic between the network and every modem connected to a given plant — was a proprietary appliance. Purpose-built hardware from a small number of suppliers handled routing, scheduling, and signal processing in dedicated silicon. Upgrading capacity meant buying and racking new boxes. Upgrading standards — from DOCSIS 2.0 to 3.0, from 3.0 to 3.1 — meant hardware replacement cycles that took years and cost hundreds of millions of dollars across a large operator.

Harmonic's CableOS product, launched commercially in the mid-2010s and put to its first major operator test with Comcast beginning in 2018, was a direct assault on that model. CableOS is a virtualised Cable Modem Termination System (vCMTS): it moves the MAC-layer functions of the traditional CMTS — scheduling, encryption, management — into software running on commodity x86 server hardware, the same class of machines that populate any hyperscale data centre. Physical-layer processing is handled by Remote PHY Devices (RPDs) distributed at the network node, completing a Distributed Access Architecture (DAA) that decouples where the signal is processed from where the intelligence lives.

The implications were consequential. A cable operator running CableOS could upgrade its access platform by pushing a software build rather than pulling and replacing rack units. Capacity could scale horizontally across additional COTS servers. Feature development — new DOCSIS modulation profiles, advanced scheduling algorithms, security patches — could cycle at software cadences rather than hardware procurement timelines. For an industry facing a generational standards transition to DOCSIS 4.0, the economics of that proposition would prove material.

## Comcast as Proving Ground, 2018–2024

Comcast, the largest cable operator in the United States, became CableOS's anchor customer and commercial proving ground. The deployment began in earnest in 2018, making Comcast one of the earliest large-scale operators to commit to a virtualised cable access architecture at production scale. By the time Patrick Harshman retired from the chief executive role in September 2023 — capping a 26-year tenure that had taken Harmonic from a video equipment manufacturer into the broadband infrastructure business — the Comcast relationship had become the defining commercial reference for the entire vCMTS category.

The scaling trajectory through this period reshaped Harmonic's financial profile. Revenue grew from $384 million in 2019 to a peak of $646 million in 2022, a climb driven substantially by CableOS deployment volume at Comcast as the operator expanded the platform across its footprint. The Broadband segment, essentially coterminous with CableOS, became the company's growth engine, while the legacy Video business continued to generate stable cash flow from a global base of broadcasters and media customers.

Revenue climbed from $377 million in 2020 to $646 million in 2022 as the Comcast deployment scaled, before moderating to $580 million in 2024 as the initial rollout phase completed (see Financial Deep Dive for the detailed trajectory).

## DOCSIS 4.0: The Upgrade Cycle That Defines the Decade

The cable industry's transition to DOCSIS 4.0 is not a single product launch — it is a multi-year, capital-intensive infrastructure programme that will determine which operators can credibly compete with fibre-to-the-home networks on symmetric multi-gigabit broadband. Two technical paths exist under the DOCSIS 4.0 umbrella: Extended Spectrum DOCSIS (ESD), which expands the upstream spectrum to 684 MHz or 1.2 GHz on existing coaxial plant, and Full Duplex DOCSIS (FDX), which enables simultaneous upstream and downstream transmission across the same spectral band. Both demand significant changes to plant infrastructure and, critically, to the access platform software.

This is where Harmonic's architecture thesis converges with a once-in-a-decade industry cycle. An operator running legacy proprietary CMTS hardware that wishes to support DOCSIS 4.0 must, in most cases, replace that hardware — a process involving substantial capital outlay and complex field operations. An operator running CableOS on COTS servers can, in principle, receive DOCSIS 4.0 capability through software updates applied to existing hardware, with incremental server additions to handle additional capacity. The distinction is not absolute — Remote PHY Device upgrades and plant electronics still require physical work — but the software-defined architecture compresses a significant portion of the upgrade cost and timeline.

CEO Nimrod Ben-Natan, who had led the CableOS product line before his February 2024 succession, brought operational continuity at a moment when the DOCSIS 4.0 transition was moving from planning to procurement.

> "The DOCSIS 4.0 transition is a multi-year opportunity, and our software-based architecture positions us to be the platform of choice as operators plan their next-generation deployments."

The operator universe's pace of DOCSIS 4.0 commitment has remained a key variable for Harmonic's Broadband segment revenue trajectory. Charter Communications, which operates under the Spectrum brand and represents the second-largest US cable operator, has engaged with next-generation access planning, and its decisions alongside those of mid-tier operators will shape Harmonic's revenue cadence through the latter half of the decade.

## The Video Segment — A Parallel Business in Motion

The Video segment — software-based video processing and delivery for broadcasters and streaming platforms — was announced for separation in 2024, allowing each business to be evaluated and managed independently (see Snapshot for the MediaKind transaction details).

The revenue contraction from the 2022 peak to $580 million in 2024 reflected deployment phasing rather than competitive loss. Whether the broader operator base accelerates into DOCSIS 4.0 spending will determine if this represents a trough or a sustained plateau.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, Comcast concentration, and the post-separation framework
chapters.body:
## A Six-Year Arc Shaped by One Customer

Few revenue curves in enterprise technology tell as concentrated a story as Harmonic's between 2019 and 2024. The company that Patrick Harshman had spent two decades reshaping from a hardware-dependent video infrastructure vendor into a software-defined cable access platform reached its commercial inflection point not through broad market diffusion but through the progressive scaling of a single relationship: Comcast.

The aggregate revenue trajectory across the six-year period was one of sharp acceleration followed by measured contraction:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD M) | YoY Change |
|-------------|-----------------|------------|
| 2019 | $384 | — |
| 2020 | $377 | −1.8% |
| 2021 | $499 | +32.4% |
| 2022 | $646 | +29.5% |
| 2023 | $610 | −5.6% |
| 2024 | $580 | −4.9% |

*Source: [Harmonic Investor Relations / SEC EDGAR CIK 0000851310](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)*

The 2019 and 2020 figures — $384 million and $377 million respectively — represent the late-incumbent phase: a company that had already committed to virtualised cable access through CableOS but had not yet translated that commitment into top-line scale. The Comcast CableOS deployment, which dated to initial commercial trials in 2018, was still in limited rollout by then, generating engineering-services and early-licence revenue that moved the mix at the margin without yet dominating reported figures.

The inflection came in 2021, when revenue climbed thirty-two percent to $499 million. That move reflected a meaningful step-up in Comcast deployment cadence — the transition from trial to scaled production across a growing number of Comcast nodes. The gains in the Broadband segment, which houses the CableOS platform, absorbed the structural pressures in the Video segment, where secular headwinds from broadcaster consolidation and the migration of linear production budgets toward streaming were already compressing the customer base.

## The Peak and the Pullback

The 2022 peak of $646 million marked the high-water mark of the initial Comcast deployment wave. In practical terms, the Comcast relationship had by that point scaled sufficiently to represent a dominant share of Broadband segment revenue. Harmonic's annual filings with the [Securities and Exchange Commission](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310) disclosed Comcast as a customer accounting for more than ten percent of consolidated revenue — a threshold that, given the CableOS deployment profile, understated the operational dependency considerably. Within the Broadband segment specifically, Comcast was the principal contributor across software licences, SaaS fees, and associated professional services.

The subsequent declines — to $610 million in 2023 and $580 million in 2024 — were not, in management's framing, evidence of platform deterioration. Rather, they reflected a natural rhythm in large-operator infrastructure programmes: an initial deployment wave generates elevated capital spending, followed by an absorption period during which the operator digests installed capacity before authorising the next tranche. Harshman, in the final quarters of his twenty-six-year tenure before his September 2023 retirement, repeatedly characterised Comcast's programme as multi-year in scope and explicitly tied the forward demand context to the DOCSIS 4.0 technology transition cycle then beginning to take shape across the US cable industry.

The concentration dynamic, however, was structurally notable. A company of Harmonic's size — sub-$650 million in peak revenue, San Jose-headquartered, listed on NASDAQ as HLIT — carrying a customer relationship of Comcast's scale created a bilateral dependency that shaped both commercial negotiations and investor perception. Positive Comcast programme updates produced meaningful stock movements; any signal of deployment deferral or volume softness had the inverse effect. The company's disclosures in successive 10-K filings acknowledged this concentration risk explicitly, as required under SEC rules, and the investor relations narrative over the 2021-2024 period was in considerable measure a running commentary on Comcast deployment phase and pace.

## Financing the Transition: Convertible Instruments

Funding the platform's build-out required capital markets access beyond what organic cash generation supported. Harmonic approached its convertible debt structure in two tranches that bracketed the peak revenue years.

In March 2019 — the same year the Comcast CableOS deployment was graduating from trial to commercial — Harmonic issued $115 million of 2.0% Convertible Senior Notes due 2024. The instrument gave the company five years of fixed-rate financing at a cost below what traditional term debt would have required, in exchange for giving noteholders an equity conversion right at a premium to the then-prevailing share price. For a company at an early-commercialisation stage, it was a structurally appropriate mechanism: it preserved liquidity for platform investment while deferring equity dilution to a period when, ideally, CableOS revenue would have matured the equity value enough to make conversion economically logical for holders.

By 2021, with the revenue trajectory validating the CableOS thesis and equity markets in a receptive posture for growth-infrastructure names, Harmonic returned to the convertible market at scale. The company issued $230 million of 1.75% Convertible Senior Notes due 2026, using a portion of the proceeds to retire the shorter-dated 2024 notes while net-adding to its liquidity position. The 2021 transaction extended the debt maturity profile by two years and modestly reduced the coupon, capturing the rate environment of that moment. It also provided a balance-sheet cushion heading into what would prove to be the peak deployment years — ensuring that incremental Comcast programme demands on engineering resources, professional services headcount, and working capital could be met without returning to capital markets under potentially less favourable conditions.

The combined convertible stack — and the subsequent 2024 maturity on the original notes — gave the incoming Ben-Natan administration a defined liability horizon against which to plan the Video separation and post-separation capital structure. With the 2026 notes outstanding and the strategic refocusing underway, the treasury question of how to capitalise a standalone Broadband entity became one of the more consequential items on the new CEO's agenda from his February 2024 first day.

## The Separation Framework

The 2024 announcement to separate the Video segment was framed by management as a value-unlocking exercise rather than a divestiture of distress. The Video business — software-based video processing, encoding, and delivery infrastructure sold to broadcasters, streaming platforms, and pay-TV operators — had been Harmonic's original franchise and remained a material revenue contributor through the dossier period. But within a consolidated Harmonic, the Video segment's secular growth profile, its customer base, and its capital requirements were structurally mismatched with those of CableOS.

The separation rationale operated on two levels. First, a standalone Video entity would be valued by public markets on its own terms — recurring software revenue, broadcaster consolidation dynamics, the shift toward cloud-based production — without the noise of a high-growth cable infrastructure platform distorting the multiple. Second, a standalone Broadband entity would be free to pursue the capital structure, partnership strategy, and go-to-market posture that the DOCSIS 4.0 transition demanded, without the organisational complexity of running two businesses with fundamentally different customers, cycles, and competitive dynamics.

The financial framework of the separation, as disclosed in the period ending at the dossier's frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, required Harmonic to report the two segments with sufficient stand-alone detail to support investor modelling of the post-separation entities. Within the Broadband segment, Comcast-related revenue — spanning SaaS subscription fees, software licences, and professional services — was the dominant line item, and the forward CableOS growth narrative was anchored to the multi-year DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle that cable operators across North America were beginning to fund. Charter Communications was cited alongside Comcast as a material broadband customer, providing at least a degree of diversification beyond the single-anchor dependency.

Within Video, the customer base was structurally more distributed — broadcasters, streaming platforms, and regional pay-TV operators across multiple continents — but the revenue was growing more slowly and faced secular pressure from the same forces compressing the global linear television complex. The separation, in that sense, was also an acknowledgement that those two customer bases and those two growth profiles were better served by dedicated management focus than by the administrative co-existence that a diversified Harmonic had maintained for a decade.

## Ben-Natan's Inherited Ledger

When Nimrod Ben-Natan formally assumed the chief executive role in February 2024, following Walter Jankovic's brief interim stewardship after Harshman's September 2023 retirement, the financial inheritance was a company generating approximately $580 million in annual revenue with a concentration risk in its highest-growth segment, a convertible debt maturity approaching in 2026, and a separation process in active execution. Ben-Natan's prior role as SVP and General Manager of the Cable Edge business — the CableOS group — meant he arrived with direct knowledge of the Comcast programme's technical status and commercial cadence, a credential that was explicitly part of the board's rationale for the internal succession.

The revenue trajectory from 2019 to 2024 had demonstrated that CableOS could scale from pilot to production at a tier-one operator and generate transformative revenue growth. The $262 million gross revenue gain between the 2019 trough and the 2022 peak was almost entirely a Broadband segment story, and the Broadband segment story was almost entirely a Comcast story. The task confronting Ben-Natan was to convert that proof-of-concept concentration into a diversified cable-industry franchise in time for the DOCSIS 4.0 capital spending cycle — while simultaneously executing a segment separation that would reshape the company's financial architecture from the ground up.

The ledger he inherited was not a failing one. But it was unambiguously a ledger shaped by a single commercial relationship, funded by convertible instruments timed to a specific deployment hypothesis, and now requiring a structural reset to realise the next phase of its platform ambitions.

chapters.title: Post-Harshman quarters through Ben-Natan succession and Video announcement
chapters.body:
## The Final Harshman Quarters

Patrick Harshman had spent more than a quarter-century building Harmonic into the infrastructure layer beneath the world's cable networks. His departure in September 2023, after twenty-six years as president and chief executive, came not in crisis but in the quieter cadence of succession — a transition announced and managed, the founder-era CEO stepping back as the company he had remade around virtualised cable access approached a new inflection point.

The financial record of his final years was not a clean crescendo. Revenue reached [$646 million in 2022](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com), the peak of the CableOS deployment ramp at Comcast and the broader operator base, then retreated to approximately [$610 million in 2023](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) as the initial scaling phase at the principal cable customer moderated. The pattern was familiar to anyone who had followed the company since the 2018 Comcast deployment began: Harmonic's Broadband segment revenues moved in irregular pulses tied to capital-expenditure cycles at a concentrated customer base, not in the smooth quarterly progressions that analysts preferred. Harshman had spent years educating investors in that dynamic. His successor would inherit both the framework and its complications.

## Jankovic Holds the Bridge

Walter Jankovic stepped into the interim chief-executive role in September 2023 as the board initiated a formal succession process. The CFO's elevation was a deliberate stabilisation choice: Jankovic knew the financial architecture of the company intimately, held the confidence of the institutional shareholder base, and carried no ambiguity about the temporary nature of the role. His mandate was continuity — maintaining the Comcast relationship, keeping the Video segment on its operational path, and delivering clean quarterly disclosures while the board completed its search.

The search, as it turned out, did not require a lengthy external sweep. The candidate the board settled on had been inside Harmonic since 1999.

## Ben-Natan's Succession: February 2024

Nimrod Ben-Natan was appointed president and chief executive officer in February 2024, and Jankovic returned to the chief financial officer seat he had vacated five months earlier. The symmetry of that return was itself a signal: the board had sought not disruption but depth.

Ben-Natan's path to the chief executive role ran through DiviCom, the Israeli video-technology company he co-founded and whose 1999 acquisition by Harmonic brought him into the organisation. Over the subsequent two and a half decades he moved through senior product and operating roles before becoming senior vice president and general manager of the Cable Edge business — the internal designation for the CableOS product line. He had, in effect, been running the franchise that defined Harmonic's forward strategy before he was asked to run the company.

The Cable Edge appointment made the succession logic transparent. CableOS was Harmonic's central commercial bet: a virtualised, software-native replacement for the proprietary CMTS hardware that cable operators had deployed for decades. The Comcast deployment, which began in 2018 and expanded steadily through the following years, was the proof-of-concept at the scale that mattered. Ben-Natan had been the operational steward of that programme before assuming the CEO role. The board was not installing a new strategy; it was installing the person most closely identified with executing the existing one.

Bart Spriester moved into the Cable Access general manager role that Ben-Natan vacated, providing continuity within the CableOS organisation. Jay Stein remained as chief technology officer, and Robert Folliard continued to lead the Video segment organisation.

## Revenue in the Transition Window

The quarterly record across the transition period reflected the structural dynamics of a company whose primary growth driver was tied to a single large customer's deployment calendar. Full-year revenue fell from [$610 million in 2023](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) to approximately [$580 million in 2024](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) — a further contraction that, taken in isolation, appeared to tell a story of decline.

Revenue fell from the $646 million 2022 peak to $610 million in 2023 and $580 million in 2024 — a normalisation in Comcast deployment cadence rather than competitive erosion. The structural point in Ben-Natan's first year was the approaching DOCSIS 4.0 capital-expenditure wave.

## The Video Separation Announcement

The parallel 2024 announcement to separate the Video segment reflected strategic clarity implicit in the CableOS investment thesis: a company with a legacy video business and a high-growth broadband platform carried a conglomerate discount. The post-separation entity would be a pure-play CableOS company.

## Governance Through the Transition

Chairman Patrick Gallagher, appointed in 2022, presided over continuity of board leadership through the succession. Harshman remained on the board following his retirement, preserving institutional memory. Ben-Natan inherited a company mid-transformation — revenues compressing, a segment separation in progress, and the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle not yet generating the next ramp.

chapters.title: Ben-Natan, Jankovic, segment leadership, and Gallagher-chaired board
chapters.body:
## Succession by Design

The appointment of Nimrod Ben-Natan as President and Chief Executive Officer of Harmonic in February 2024 was less a hiring decision than the activation of a long-assembled capability. Ben-Natan had spent the better part of a quarter century inside the company, arriving through the 1999 acquisition of DiviCom — the Israeli multimedia encoding and transport startup he had helped build — and working his way through every level of product and operating leadership before landing in the role that mattered most heading into the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle: Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Cable Edge business, the internal organisation responsible for CableOS. When Patrick Gallagher, the non-executive Chairman, formally announced the succession, the board was not installing an outsider to arrest a crisis. It was handing the keys to the engineer who had designed the engine.

The transition unfolded in stages across the autumn and winter of 2023-2024. Patrick Harshman, who had led Harmonic for twenty-six years — from 1997 through September 2023 — retired from the chief executive role in a planned succession. Chief Financial Officer Walter Jankovic held the interim CEO position through the bridge period, maintaining financial discipline and operational continuity while the board completed its process. Ben-Natan's formal assumption of the presidency followed in February 2024, with Jankovic reverting to the CFO seat he had occupied before the interregnum. The structure that resulted — a product-native CEO, a battle-tested CFO, and a chairman with deep telecommunications operating experience — reflected the demands of a company executing simultaneously on the largest commercial deployment in its history, at Comcast, while engineering the formal separation of its legacy Video segment.

## Ben-Natan: Twenty-Five Years to the CEO Chair

Born in Israel and trained in computer science at Tel Aviv University, Ben-Natan came to Harmonic at thirty-two years old as part of the DiviCom transaction. [Harmonic Inc. Leadership](https://www.harmonicinc.com/company/leadership/) DiviCom had been a meaningful force in digital video encoding and MPEG transport infrastructure during the late-1990s satellite and cable build-out; its acquisition broadened Harmonic's product line at precisely the moment that digital television infrastructure was scaling globally. Ben-Natan stayed.

What followed was an operating career of unusual continuity for a technology executive in Silicon Valley. Through the company's Video-centric years — the broadcast and satellite era that defined Harmonic through the 2000s and into the 2010s — Ben-Natan accumulated product and programme experience across encoding, delivery, and network processing. His positioning shifted decisively when Harmonic made its bet on virtualised cable access. The CableOS initiative, which culminated in the landmark 2018 commercial deployment agreement with Comcast, required an organisational nerve centre capable of translating software architecture into cable-plant operations at scale. Ben-Natan was given that responsibility as SVP/GM of the Cable Edge business. In practice, this meant he ran the product line — engineering, product management, customer deployment, and roadmap — through the period when Comcast was integrating CableOS into its network and the broader cable industry was beginning to evaluate virtualised CMTS alternatives.

That background gave the February 2024 succession an asymmetric quality. Ben-Natan assumed the CEO role with a granular, operational understanding of the technology stack and the customer relationships that constituted the company's primary growth thesis. He was not arriving to assess an unfamiliar business: he had built the relevant portion of it. The mandate at succession was direct: sustain and extend the Comcast deployment, accelerate penetration among the broader cable operator customer base, and manage the structural evolution of the company — which included the planned separation of the Video segment that Harmonic had announced in 2024.

## Jankovic and the CFO Anchor

Walter Jankovic's career arc is the mirror image of Ben-Natan's in one important respect: where the CEO's strength is product-native depth in a single company, the CFO brings a cross-industry operating biography accumulated across several hardware-intensive technology cycles. [Harmonic Inc. Leadership](https://www.harmonicinc.com/company/leadership/) Before returning to Harmonic's CFO seat, Jankovic held financial leadership positions at Lumentum, Oclaro, and Celestica — three companies whose fortunes tracked different phases of the optical networking and electronics manufacturing supply chains. He holds an M.A. in Accounting from the University of Waterloo and carries a CPA designation. The aggregate spans roughly thirty years.

The interim CEO period was brief — roughly four months between Harshman's September 2023 retirement and Ben-Natan's February 2024 appointment — but its significance was not trivial. Jankovic's willingness to serve in an acting capacity, and his orderly return to the CFO role when the permanent successor was named, established a tone of institutional stability during a period when the company was simultaneously navigating a CEO change, a major commercial deployment, and the early planning stages of a segment separation. For analysts and investors, the message carried in the structure was clear: the management team was not improvising.

As CFO in the Ben-Natan era, Jankovic carries the financial architecture of a company in transition. The Video segment separation — announced in 2024 and progressing through the frozen window toward a planned divestiture — imposes material demands on the finance function: carve-out accounting, standalone cost structure modelling, and the capital-markets interface for a transaction that, if completed, would leave Harmonic as a pure-play broadband software company. Jankovic also manages the investor relationship alongside Ben-Natan, communicating a guidance framework to an equity market that, by the time of the frozen snapshot in May 2026, had extended the stock to approximately $15.20 per share against a fifty-two-week low of $7.80 — a doubling off the trough that reflected growing conviction in the broadband segment's commercial trajectory.

## Gallagher Chairs; Harshman Remains

Patrick J. Gallagher has occupied the board's chairmanship since 2022, arriving with a career biography rooted in the telecommunications operating world that Harmonic's CableOS business is now reshaping. A former senior executive at Sprint Corporation, Gallagher brought to the chairmanship an understanding of large-scale network infrastructure, carrier economics, and the organisational complexity of technology transitions inside incumbent operators — precisely the environment in which Harmonic's cable operator customers are operating. [Harmonic Governance](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com/governance) His tenure as non-executive Chair has encompassed both of the major governance events of the past three years: the Harshman retirement and the Jankovic-to-Ben-Natan succession.

The Gallagher chairmanship's structural function during the succession was to provide stable governance continuity while the CEO seat was in transition. The Chairman's role in such periods is largely invisible when executed well; a CEO transition that produces no visible governance turbulence is itself evidence of a functioning board. That Harmonic moved through the Harshman-to-Ben-Natan transition without operational disruption — maintaining its Comcast deployment commitments and its financial communication cadence through the bridge period — reflects, in part, the board oversight that Gallagher provided.

Patrick Harshman's continuing presence on the board as a non-executive director, following his September 2023 retirement from the CEO role, is the most strategically significant single board composition decision of the transition period. A CEO who led an organisation for twenty-six years accumulates a depth of customer relationship history, institutional memory, and product knowledge that cannot be replicated from the outside. Harshman was present at Harmonic's transformation from a digital video encoding equipment supplier into a software-driven cable broadband infrastructure company; his board continuity gives Ben-Natan access, in the boardroom, to the full longitudinal context of that transformation. The arrangement is uncommon only in its degree: the former CEO as director is a governance structure that in theory creates awkwardness, but in a company executing on a multi-year technology deployment of the complexity and scale of CableOS, the institutional continuity benefit is material.

## Segment Operators and the Legal Function

Below the CEO and CFO level, Harmonic's operating structure as of the frozen window aligns executive accountability to its two reportable business segments. Bart Spriester, as Senior Vice President and General Manager of Cable Access, leads the CableOS product line organisation — the team responsible for the virtualised CMTS technology, the Comcast deployment programme, and the broader customer-facing operations of the Broadband segment. Spriester stepped into the role that Ben-Natan vacated on his elevation to CEO, inheriting a product line that had become the company's predominant revenue driver and its primary investment thesis for the capital markets.

Robert Folliard, as Senior Vice President for Video, leads the segment that Harmonic announced its intention to separate. The Video business — software-based video processing and delivery infrastructure for media customers — has its own customer relationships, technology roadmap, and cost structure, and Folliard's operational remit through the transition period has been simultaneously to maintain commercial performance and to prepare the segment for standalone operation. That combination is demanding; managing a business unit toward a divestiture while preserving customer confidence and employee continuity requires a specific kind of operational steadiness.

Jay Stein, as Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer, provides the technology leadership function across both segments — a role whose scope narrows, in theory, once the Video segment is separated, but which during the transition carries the full product architecture responsibilities of the current dual-segment structure. Timothy Chu, as General Counsel, Senior Vice President of Human Resources, and Corporate Secretary, manages the legal and compliance framework; in the context of the Video separation, Chu's function encompasses the transaction structuring, contractual carve-out work, and regulatory interface that a divestiture of this complexity demands.

## Board Architecture for a Bifurcating Company

The seven-member board that Gallagher chairs represents a composition calibrated, broadly, to the company's current strategic moment. Beyond Gallagher (telecommunications operating background), Ben-Natan (executive director), and Harshman (multi-decade Harmonic institutional continuity), the independent directors bring a range of industry perspectives. Mitzi Reaugh contributes media and broadcast sector experience — directly relevant to the Video segment and its customer base of broadcasters and streaming operators, including through the separation process. Susan G. Swenson offers technology-industry CEO experience from prior public-company operating roles. David Krall adds technology-company executive depth. E. Floyd Kvamme, a long-tenured technology-sector venture capital veteran, brings the pattern recognition of someone who has watched multiple technology platform transitions from the capital formation side.

The composition does not attempt to be a telecommunications-engineering board; it is a governance body calibrated to oversee a company navigating a specific set of strategic inflections — a major commercial deployment at scale, a segment separation, a management succession, and a multi-year DOCSIS 4.0 cycle that is expected to drive continued demand for virtualised cable access infrastructure. Against those parameters, the pairing of Gallagher's carrier-side network infrastructure experience, Harshman's Harmonic-specific institutional knowledge, and Reaugh's Video-customer-base perspective covers the principal board-level oversight dimensions of the 2024-2026 period.

chapters.title: Comcast, Charter, broader cable operators, broadcasters, and supply chain
chapters.body:
The commercial relationship between Harmonic and Comcast Cable — the largest cable operator in the United States — defined the CableOS franchise as much as the technology itself. When Comcast agreed to deploy Harmonic's virtualised cable modem termination system at scale beginning in 2018, it did so under terms that bound the two companies far more tightly than a standard vendor agreement: Comcast received warrants to acquire Harmonic common stock, a structure that aligned the operator's financial interest with the success of the deployment and gave Wall Street a durable signal of commitment.

## The Comcast Commercial Architecture

The commercial agreement, disclosed in Harmonic's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission ([CIK 0000851310](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)), gave Comcast the right to purchase a meaningful stake in Harmonic at fixed strike prices tied to deployment milestones. The arrangement was unusual in enterprise software — closer to a strategic partnership underwriting than a procurement contract — and it reflected the degree to which the CableOS deployment represented existential stakes for Harmonic. A successful Comcast rollout would validate the virtualised access platform model; a stumble would imperil the entire broadband thesis.

By 2022, when Harmonic reported $646 million in full-year revenue, the Comcast deployment had scaled to become the anchor contributor to the Broadband segment. The operator's cable plant — spanning millions of homes passed across markets including the Philadelphia region and parts of the Southeast — served as the living proof-of-concept for CableOS, demonstrating that a software-based vCMTS running on commercial off-the-shelf hardware could replace purpose-built cable access equipment at carrier scale. That demonstration carried commercial weight beyond Comcast itself: every cable engineering team watching the deployment was effectively watching a reference architecture take shape.

Comcast's concentration within Harmonic's revenue base also carried risk. Annual filings repeatedly identified the operator as a customer whose decisions — on deployment cadence, technology refresh cycles, or vendor selection — could materially affect revenue. The revenue contraction from $646 million (2022) to $580 million (2024) reflected the lumpiness inherent in a deployment model where a single anchor customer's capital spending programme swings quarterly results.

## Charter Communications and the Broader US Cable Market

Charter Communications, the second-largest US cable operator by subscriber count, emerged as a significant CableOS customer as the DOCSIS 4.0 transition gathered momentum. Charter's network evolution strategy — oriented around multi-gigabit broadband ambitions and competitive response to fibre overbuilders — aligned with the virtualised access platform's promise of software-upgradeable capacity and reduced per-bit operating cost. Harmonic's filings listed Charter among its principal customers, and the operator's engagement provided the commercial validation that the CableOS franchise was not a single-operator phenomenon dependent on Comcast's continued patronage.

The broader US cable market presented Harmonic with a structural growth opportunity tied to the industry's technology replacement cycle. DOCSIS 4.0, the standard governing next-generation data-over-cable transmission, required meaningful capital investment by operators seeking to compete with fibre-to-the-home deployments by telephone companies. The virtualised approach that CableOS represented — decoupling the software intelligence from proprietary hardware — offered operators a path to DOCSIS 4.0 capability without the long lead-time hardware procurement cycles that had characterised prior generations of cable infrastructure.

Mid-tier US operators — those running regional cable systems with hundreds of thousands rather than millions of subscribers — represented a third tier of potential CableOS customers that Harmonic addressed through its direct sales organisation. These operators typically lacked the in-house engineering bench of a Comcast or Charter but faced identical competitive pressures from fibre incumbents and fixed wireless access providers. For them, the managed-software model of CableOS, in which Harmonic's engineering team carries the burden of platform maintenance and feature delivery, held particular appeal: they could adopt carrier-grade virtualised infrastructure without building the headcount to operate it.

## International Cable Operators

Harmonic's Broadband segment extended beyond North America to cable operators across Europe and Latin America. European cable markets — where operators including Liberty Global's regional subsidiaries ran large-scale hybrid fibre-coaxial networks — offered deployment opportunities as those operators contemplated their own transitions toward higher-capacity access standards. Latin American operators, in markets characterised by rapid broadband subscriber growth and more constrained capital budgets, represented a different demand profile: cost efficiency and deployment flexibility mattered more than outright peak throughput.

The international customer base provided Harmonic with geographic diversification that partially offset the concentration risk embedded in the Comcast relationship. International deployments also served a commercial purpose beyond direct revenue: they broadened the ecosystem of operators running CableOS, generating operational data and use cases that Harmonic's engineering teams incorporated into subsequent platform releases. In markets where regulatory or spectrum conditions differed from the United States, international deployments tested CableOS configurations that enriched the platform's feature set for the global operator community.

## Video Segment: Broadcasters and Media Customers

The Video segment — the business line that predated CableOS and that Harmonic's founders built through the company's early decades — served a distinct customer universe: broadcasters, streaming platforms, satellite operators, and sports rights holders requiring software-based video compression, processing, and delivery infrastructure. Names across the spectrum of global broadcast and pay-television appeared in the customer base, from national public broadcasters in Europe to North American sports networks to streaming services deploying cloud-native video pipelines.

The Video segment's customer relationships tended to be project-driven and technology-refresh-dependent: a broadcaster upgrading from standard-definition to high-definition infrastructure, or a streaming service transitioning its encoding pipeline to HEVC or AV1, represented a discrete revenue event rather than a recurring platform subscription. That structure produced a different revenue cadence than the Broadband segment's deployment contracts and contributed to the strategic logic behind Harmonic's 2024 announcement that it would separate the Video business as a standalone entity.

The separation announcement signalled that Harmonic's leadership — with Nimrod Ben-Natan installed as chief executive in February 2024 — viewed the two businesses as serving sufficiently different customer bases, capital requirements, and technology trajectories that operating them within a single public company imposed costs on both. For Video customers, a standalone entity would carry clearer strategic focus unencumbered by cable broadband capital allocation decisions; for Broadband customers, the separated company would carry an equity story undiluted by Video's distinct growth profile.

## Semiconductor and Component Supply Chain

Harmonic's virtualised access platform model carried a supply chain profile meaningfully different from that of traditional cable equipment vendors. Because CableOS ran on commercial off-the-shelf server hardware rather than proprietary application-specific integrated circuits, Harmonic's semiconductor exposure ran through the broader merchant silicon ecosystem — Intel, AMD, and the network interface card suppliers whose components populated the servers that operators deployed in cable headends and hub sites.

The global semiconductor supply disruptions of 2021 and 2022 — which compressed inventory across the technology hardware sector — affected Harmonic's ability to fulfil hardware-related orders and contributed to the revenue dynamics of that period. Harmonic's filings disclosed supply chain risk as a factor in operational planning, and the company worked to extend supply commitments and diversify component sourcing to reduce single-supplier dependencies.

Over time, the shift toward a software-centric revenue model — in which software licences and SaaS-style platform fees represented a growing proportion of Broadband segment revenue — reduced, though did not eliminate, Harmonic's sensitivity to component availability. Software-only deployments, in which the operator supplied its own server infrastructure, sidestepped hardware supply constraints entirely. That architectural flexibility became a commercial argument in its own right: an operator facing hardware lead-time pressures could begin a CableOS deployment on existing or separately sourced hardware while Harmonic's software team managed integration and platform delivery.

The supply chain architecture also reinforced Harmonic's asset-light ambitions. Where traditional cable equipment vendors carried manufacturing facilities, component inventories, and logistics infrastructure, Harmonic's model pushed much of that burden to hardware vendor partners and, increasingly, to the operators themselves. The resulting capital efficiency — visible in the company's balance sheet relative to peers carrying heavier manufacturing footprints — reinforced the investment case that Ben-Natan and his predecessor Patrick Harshman had articulated across the decade-long CableOS build-out: a software company that happened to sell into cable, not a hardware company seeking a software veneer.

chapters.title: Where Harmonic sits against Cisco, CommScope, Vecima, Arista, and the broader cable access
chapters.body:
By the time Nimrod Ben-Natan settled into the chief executive's chair in February 2024, the competitive map of cable access had already shifted in ways that his decade running the CableOS product line had helped engineer. The market Harmonic entered as a niche challenger in the mid-2010s had, by the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, reorganised itself around three vectors: a dominant vCMTS incumbent measured in tens of millions of managed cable modems, a distressed hardware-era giant scrambling to acquire its way into virtualisation, and a Canadian specialist collecting its first meaningful vCMTS revenue cheques. A fourth player — Cisco Systems — had effectively left the field.

## The Incumbent That Retreated: Cisco

For most of the DOCSIS 3.0 and 3.1 era, Cisco's cBR-8 Converged Broadband Router stood as the industry's reference CMTS platform. Cable operators from Comcast to mid-size regional MSOs standardised on it. The machine was well-engineered, well-supported, and, by the time DOCSIS 4.0 arrived on the horizon, a dead end. The cBR-8 carried no upgrade path to DOCSIS 4.0; the hardware architecture that made it reliable in one generation became a liability in the next.

Cisco did attempt a software-defined answer. Its cloud-native broadband router and SmartPHY virtual CMTS were developed under John Chapman, a DOCSIS pioneer whose departure from Cisco marked, in the view of industry observers, the symbolic close of the company's cable ambitions. By 2023, Cisco had quietly mothballed its vCMTS programme. The company that once held the largest share of cable headend equipment was, by 2024, no longer an active bidder for new CMTS contracts.

The vacuum this created was substantial. Harmonic's then-SVP Ben-Natan told industry publication Light Reading in 2023 that Harmonic was "poised to pass Cisco in CMTS market share" — a claim that had become plainly settled fact by the time he became CEO. Research firm Dell'Oro Group credited Harmonic with roughly 98 per cent of global vCMTS revenue as of year-end 2023. That is not market leadership in the ordinary sense; it is category ownership.

## CommScope: The Debt-Laden Incumbent Buys Its Way In

The more consequential competitive story was playing out at CommScope. The company had absorbed Arris International — and its storied E6000 Converged Edge Router legacy — in a 2019 transaction valued at approximately $7.4 billion. The deal saddled CommScope with a debt load that would define its strategic options for the next six years.

By 2024, CommScope was being categorised alongside Lumen Technologies and Dish Network as one of the most financially distressed equipment companies in the sector. Talks with an ad hoc creditor group collapsed in November 2024 without resolution. What followed was a $3.15 billion first-lien term loan and $1 billion first-lien notes refinancing, arranged through Apollo Global Management and Monarch Alternative Capital, to retire nearer-term maturities. The company did not file for bankruptcy, but the exercise demonstrated how little financial slack it carried into the DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle.

Its strategic answer to the virtualisation gap arrived in May 2024, when a bankruptcy court in Delaware auctioned the cable assets of Casa Systems. CommScope bid $45.1 million — outpacing Vecima Networks' $44.95 million stalking-horse offer — to acquire the Axyom vCMTS platform, along with Casa's fibre nodes and I-CMTS chassis. Axyom carried a modest but real production footprint: commercial deployments at Rogers Communications in Canada and Claro Colombia. Dell'Oro Group concluded that the acquisition positioned CommScope as the number-two vCMTS player globally, though it noted that both CommScope and Vecima had "lagged behind Harmonic" before the Casa deal closed.

CommScope also retained credible momentum in the physical-layer DOCSIS 4.0 market. Its vCCAP Evo cloud-native CCAP platform — capable of delivering up to 180 gigabits per second per rack unit on commodity Intel servers — won a significant European reference contract in June 2025, when Liberty Global selected vCCAP Evo alongside CommScope's DC2182 DOCSIS 4.0 1.8 GHz DAA nodes for upgrades at VodafoneZiggo, Telenet and Sunrise. That deployment covers the Netherlands, Belgium and Switzerland and represented one of the larger DOCSIS 4.0 contract announcements visible in the research window. Full-year 2024 revenue across CommScope landed at $4.21 billion, down 7.9 per cent year on year, though the Access Network Solutions division posted 11.8 per cent growth in the final quarter of 2024.

The balance-sheet story was not finished. In 2025, CommScope announced the $10.5 billion sale of its Connectivity and Cable Solutions passive-infrastructure segment to Amphenol — a transaction aimed at extinguishing the remaining debt overhand from the Arris acquisition. Critically, the cable access business was not sold. The Access Network Solutions division, home to the E6000, vCCAP Evo and the acquired Axyom platform, was retained as the core of the post-transaction company. The Amphenol deal, pending at the snapshot date, illustrated both the severity of the balance-sheet problem and CommScope's conviction that cable access remained worth owning.

## Vecima: The Specialist Building From the Node Up

Where CommScope arrived at vCMTS via acquisition, Vecima Networks built toward it from the access node outward. The Victoria, British Columbia company had established Entra as its Distributed Access Architecture product family — Remote PHY devices, optical nodes, and amplifiers — and over the prior two years had added an Entra vCMTS to the portfolio. Introduced in March 2024, the platform was cloud-native, containerised, and interoperable with third-party RPDs including Harmonic's own.

Vecima's first commercial vCMTS revenue arrived in the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2025, ending June 2025. A more significant signal came in April 2025, when Cox Communications — a Tier 1 North American MSO — announced a multi-year agreement to deploy Entra vCMTS for next-generation DOCSIS network modernisation, with commercial ramp expected to begin in Vecima's fiscal 2026. Cox's selection of Vecima represented the only confirmed Tier 1 US cable operator vCMTS award outside Harmonic's account book visible during the research window.

Full-year fiscal 2025 revenue came in at $285.9 million, essentially flat with the prior year. Entra DAA revenue of $222.7 million grew 5 per cent year on year but gross margin compressed to 38.3 per cent from 48.7 per cent, driven by product mix and foreign-exchange headwinds. The company cited the total vCMTS market at approximately $400 million over the following three years — a figure broadly consistent with Dell'Oro Group's projection of $367 million by 2028. On those figures, Vecima was entering a market it would largely share with Harmonic and, depending on CommScope's execution post-Casa, a third competitor.

| Vendor | vCMTS Status | Key Reference Customers | DOCSIS 4.0 Ready | Capital Position |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harmonic (HLIT) | Commercial at scale; 146 deployments, 41M modems | Comcast, Charter, 140+ others | Yes — production validated | Strong; $573M backlog |
| CommScope (COMM) | Commercial via Axyom acquisition | Liberty Global, Rogers (legacy Casa) | Yes (vCCAP Evo + 1.8 GHz nodes) | Distressed; stabilising post-refi |
| Vecima (VCM) | Early commercial; first revenue Q4 FY2025 | Cox (contracted), 67 DAA MSOs | Yes (Entra vCMTS) | Revenue flat; margin under pressure |
| Cisco | Exited vCMTS | Legacy cBR-8 installed base | No | N/A for cable access |

## Arista and the Data Centre Adjacency

Arista Networks occupied a different quadrant of the conversation entirely. The San Jose networking company — $7 billion in full-year 2024 revenue, driven by hyperscale data-centre and AI-fabric switching — had no product overlap with cable access infrastructure. Its appearance in competitive analyses of Harmonic reflected a speculative thesis rather than a direct contest: as cable operators migrated headend functions to commercial cloud and edge computing infrastructure, the switching fabric inside those facilities increasingly ran on Arista hardware. CableOS, a software platform that runs on commodity servers, could in principle sit atop Arista-switched infrastructure — a vendor relationship, not a rivalry.

Whether Harmonic's software-defined cable access intellectual property could be adapted into AI data-centre or hyperscale routing applications remained, as of the snapshot date, a speculative investment thesis rather than a disclosed product roadmap. Ben-Natan did not address it explicitly in transcripts reviewed for this dossier.

## The Chinese Wall

The final competitive dimension was structural and regulatory rather than commercial. Huawei maintained a cable access product line built around DOCSIS 3.0 and 3.1 hardware, and its capacity for low-cost manufacturing had historically been cited as a long-term threat to Western equipment vendors. That threat was foreclosed in the United States when the Federal Communications Commission prohibited new equipment authorisations for Huawei products, with final rules effective in early 2023 under the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act. ZTE faced identical restrictions. No Chinese vendor appeared on any US cable operator's active vendor shortlist for the DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle. The regulatory barrier represented a permanent structural tailwind for Harmonic, CommScope and Vecima in the world's largest cable market.

## The Structural Gap

Against that backdrop, Ben-Natan's formulation on the Q4 fiscal 2025 earnings call was precise.

> "At this scale, the gap between Harmonic and the rest of the market is no longer incremental. It is structural."

The claim was arithmetically defensible. Harmonic managed more than 41 million cable modems and ONUs across 146 production deployments as of the same call. Its closest vCMTS competitor had booked its first commercial vCMTS revenue in the same quarter. Dell'Oro's historical data credited Harmonic with essentially all vCMTS revenue for the period when the market was being defined; the post-Casa CommScope and post-Cox Vecima were not so much catching up as starting the race. The DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle — with Dell'Oro projecting cumulative cable outside-plant spending of $10 billion through 2030, and 2026 expected to mark the capex rebound year after a 2025 inventory digestion pause — would test whether that structural gap was durable or merely a function of how long Harmonic had been alone on the field.

chapters.title: From 1995 IPO through CableOS, Harshman retirement, Ben-Natan succession, Video separation
chapters.body:
## The Founding Era

Harmonic, incorporated in 1988 and listed on Nasdaq in 1995 (HLIT), began as a digital video compression specialist serving broadcasters and cable headends. [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000851310](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310)

## The Harshman Era: 1997–2023

Patrick Harshman led Harmonic for 26 years, overseeing the 1999 DiviCom acquisition (which brought Nimrod Ben-Natan into the company) and the gradual shift from hardware to software-defined platforms.

## The CableOS Bet (2018)

CableOS — a virtualised CMTS running on commodity servers — began scaling at Comcast in 2018, becoming the commercial validation that transformed Harmonic from a video equipment vendor into a broadband platform company. Revenue climbed from $377 million (2020) to $646 million (2022) before moderating (see Financial Deep Dive).

## Leadership Transition (2023–2024)

Harshman retired in September 2023, remaining on the board. CFO Walter Jankovic served as interim CEO until February 2024, when Nimrod Ben-Natan — who had led the CableOS product line — was named CEO. [Harmonic IR](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com/governance) The succession installed the person most identified with the platform at the moment the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle widened the addressable opportunity.

## Video Separation (2024)

The parallel Video segment separation announcement completed the strategic posture refinement: the post-separation entity would be a pure-play broadband platform company, freeing both businesses to pursue their distinct trajectories.

chapters.title: CableOS virtualisation, DOCSIS 4.0 support, broader patents
chapters.body:
## The Virtual Stack: Software-Defined Cable Access

When Harmonic introduced CableOS in the autumn of 2016, the architecture it proposed was a fundamental departure from three decades of cable engineering convention. A cable modem termination system — the CMTS — had always been a proprietary chassis: racks of vendor-specific line cards, ASICs, and control planes locked together by the manufacturer. CableOS dissolved that hardware boundary, replacing the entire CMTS stack with software running on commercial off-the-shelf x86 servers and moving the physics of the network to standardised Remote PHY Devices at the node edge. The platform was cloud-native from an early stage, deploying containerised microservices orchestrated by Kubernetes and drawing on 4th-generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors for the signal-processing workloads that had previously demanded custom silicon.

The practical claims Harmonic made for this architecture were stark. Relative to a traditional CMTS, the company documented a 20-to-1 reduction in rack footprint and, across seven successive generations of commodity server hardware, a 75 per cent reduction in power consumption. Because the software abstracted the data plane from any specific processor, every Intel die-shrink translated automatically into additional DOCSIS capacity per rack unit — a compounding efficiency that proprietary hardware could not match.

## A Patent Foundation for the Virtualisation Era

The intellectual-property strategy that accompanied CableOS reflected the company's conviction that the virtualisation approach was architecturally novel. On 26 July 2018, the United States Patent and Trademark Office granted US Patent 10,020,962, titled "Virtual Converged Cable Access Platform (CCAP) Core." It was the first of what then-chief executive Patrick Harshman described as a broadening moat.

> "The future of cable access technology is virtualized software, and the award of this foundational patent highlights Harmonic's ground-breaking innovation and increasingly strong market position. This patent and our 94 pending patent applications, a number of which relate to our CableOS technologies, make a clear statement of our ability to solve the real-world challenges for our customers."
>
> — Patrick Harshman, press release, 26 July 2018

A second foundational patent followed on 4 December 2018: US Patent 10,104,405, covering dynamic allocation of CPU cycles in cloud-based video stream processing — a method central to Harmonic's Video-as-a-Service platform. By the time the [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000851310/000119312526067506/hlit-20251231.htm) was filed in early 2026, Harmonic's active portfolio comprised 65 issued US patents, seven issued foreign patents, and 39 pending applications across cable access virtualisation, distributed access architecture, remote PHY, and video encoding.

Two later patents illustrated how the portfolio continued to evolve alongside deployments at scale. The company's patented PTP-less timing solution — which eliminated the need for Precision Time Protocol infrastructure in distributed access networks, reducing deployment complexity and lowering operator cost — became a documented differentiator in competitive sales. Polish operator Vectra cited it explicitly when selecting Harmonic for its broadband transformation in 2025. By then, chief executive Nimrod Ben-Natan described the solution going into commercial production as delivering a concrete economic benefit:

> "our patented PTP less timing solution into live commercial service. This technology lowers overall DAA cost."
>
> — Nimrod Ben-Natan, Q1 2025 earnings call, 28 April 2025

At SCTE TechExpo 2025, Harmonic also unveiled Pathfinder, a self-healing network capability that Ben-Natan described as patent-pending, designed to detect and mitigate localised spectrum interference autonomously — a foretaste of the autonomous network intelligence layer the company began presenting as a distinct competitive dimension.

The portfolio's only significant defensive test had come from outside the cable segment entirely: Avid Technology brought two suits in Delaware between 2011 and 2017 over data-storage patents relating to Harmonic's legacy MediaGrid broadcast storage product. After the Federal Circuit ordered a retrial in 2016, the parties settled in October 2017 on terms that included a cross-licence and a cash payment from Harmonic to Avid. The dispute touched no CableOS-related technology.

## Extending the Spectrum: DOCSIS 4.0 in Two Flavours

DOCSIS 4.0 arrived in two technically distinct variants that placed different demands on operators' existing hybrid-fibre-coax plants. Extended Spectrum DOCSIS pushed the downstream spectrum ceiling to 1.2 GHz or 1.8 GHz using conventional frequency-division duplexing — a comparatively straightforward amplifier upgrade. Full Duplex DOCSIS allowed simultaneous upstream and downstream transmission within an overlapping spectrum band, offering substantially higher upstream capacity but requiring amplifiers capable of managing echo cancellation at each node. Most vendors chose to support one variant or the other.

In October 2023, Harmonic announced that its renamed cOS platform had become the first in the industry to support both FDX and ESD within a single software instance, alongside 10G passive optical network convergence.
