The capability was demonstrated in live production with Comcast, whose chief network officer Elad Nafshi noted that the virtual CMTS deployment had positioned the operator to launch "the world's first DOCSIS 4.0-powered Internet service." Harmonic's own framing emphasised the strategic latitude the unified approach gave operators:

> "The cOS platform is unique in the marketplace today, making it even easier for operators to address the very real economic, environmental and technical requirements they face, while also ensuring greater agility and versatility to strategically extend high-speed services to more subscribers."
>
> — Nimrod Ben-Natan, press release, 16 October 2023

Hardware support for the new standard was delivered through the Pebble-2 Remote PHY Device, which Harmonic characterised as the most power-efficient device in its class and which supported DOCSIS 3.1 and both DOCSIS 4.0 modes across a full 1.8 GHz spectrum. On 8 July 2025, a Pebble-2 paired with the cOS core software achieved 14 Gbps downstream throughput at a [CableLabs interoperability event](https://www.harmonicinc.com/press-releases/harmonic-14gbps-docsis4-harmonic-cablelabs-demo) — exceeding the 10 Gbps headline target associated with the standard.

Field commitments followed the technical validation. By the close of 2024, Harmonic counted ten Tier-1 operators engaged on the Unified DOCSIS 4.0 platform. The first commercial Extended Spectrum rollouts entered service in the third quarter of 2025. Vodafone Germany completed a field validation before the end of that year.

## R&D Investment and Engineering Geography

The research expenditure that underpinned both the CableOS platform and the video portfolio was sustained at elevated levels through the growth phase of the DOCSIS transition. Combined R&D reached $126.3 million in fiscal 2023 and $121.0 million in fiscal 2024, representing approximately 18–21 per cent of total revenue in each year. The company's engineering footprint spread across sites in California, Oregon, and New Jersey in the United States, alongside significant presences in France, Israel, and Hong Kong, with supplemental development resources in Ukraine and India. France, in particular, generated meaningful cost offsets: the Crédit d'Impôt Recherche programme returned between $5.4 million and $6.2 million annually in tax credits across the 2021–2023 period.

After Harmonic announced the pending sale of its Video business to MediaKind for approximately $145 million in December 2025, the Video segment was reclassified as discontinued operations, and the reported R&D figure for fiscal 2025 — against continuing broadband operations only — fell to $75.0 million, with the roughly $45–50 million attributable to video processing engineering departing with the asset. The PURE Compression Engine, which had encoded content to HEVC, AV1, and VVC standards, and the VOS 360 cloud video platform carrying its associated processing patents, transferred to MediaKind upon closing. What remained was a tighter, broadband-focused engineering organisation whose patent accumulation over the DOCSIS 4.0 era — timing solutions, self-healing automation, and the foundational virtualisation claims of 2018 — had been built entirely around the converged cable access platform that Ben-Natan had spent a quarter-century helping to create.

chapters.title: Comcast concentration, DOCSIS 4.0 cycle, competitive intensity, Video separation execution
chapters.body:
## A Narrowing Base, an Unsettled Industry

The Video segment separation concentrates Harmonic on a single business line, exposing it to structural risks previously diffused across a more diversified revenue base. Six distinct risk vectors demand attention.

---

## The Comcast Dependency

No risk figure looms larger than Harmonic's exposure to a single customer. Comcast drove the revenue surge from $377 million (2020) to $646 million (2022), and the subsequent ~10% two-year contraction mirrored the anchor customer's deployment cadence. Diversification into Charter and international operators matters at the margin, but Comcast's scale means meaningful dilution would take years. A capex pause or vendor renegotiation at Comcast creates an existential quarterly conversation.

---

## DOCSIS 4.0 Cycle Timing

The bull case for Harmonic's post-separation broadband entity rests substantially on the multi-year DOCSIS 4.0 transition. The upgrade cycle — from DOCSIS 3.1 infrastructure toward the symmetrical multi-gigabit architecture of DOCSIS 4.0 — represents the most significant network capital programme in the North American cable industry since the digital migration of the late 1990s. For a vendor whose virtualised cable modem termination system was purpose-built for software-defined, cloud-native architectures, the cycle should be generationally favourable.

The risk is not whether the cycle arrives but when, at what pace, and through which vendors. Cable operators are under simultaneous pressure from overbuilders — principally fibre-to-the-premises competitors from AT&T and independent fibre ISPs — that has accelerated the urgency of network upgrades. But urgency and capital allocation are different things. Large operators carry substantial leverage on their balance sheets and must sequence DOCSIS 4.0 alongside ongoing plant maintenance, mid-split and high-split interim upgrades, and the fixed wireless assault on their subscriber base. Any compression of operator free cash flow — whether from competitive pricing pressure or subscriber churn — compresses the capital budget from which Harmonic draws its orders.

There is also a technology sequencing risk. The industry's path to DOCSIS 4.0 runs through either Extended Spectrum DOCSIS or Full Duplex DOCSIS architectures, each with distinct infrastructure implications. Operators that choose a slower or more incremental upgrade path may delay material CableOS procurement even as the headline DOCSIS 4.0 narrative remains intact. Harmonic's revenue does not accrue from the announcement of industry roadmaps; it accrues from signed purchase orders and deployments.

---

## Competitive Intensity

CableOS's early-mover window has narrowed. CommScope (via ARRIS heritage and the Casa Systems acquisition) and Vecima Networks now field credible vCMTS alternatives, and cable operators have strong incentives to maintain at least two qualified vendors. Ben-Natan's team must sustain technical differentiation against products that are now, unlike in 2018, genuinely capable and commercially referenced. (See Competitive Position for detailed vendor analysis.)

---

## Video Separation Execution

Separations require sustained management attention — carve-out accounting, duplicated shared services, renegotiated customer relationships — at exactly the moment Ben-Natan is managing a CEO transition, the Comcast relationship, and a more crowded competitive market. The execution risk is heightened by contracting revenue: separating a business amid declining consolidated results limits the financial cushion for costs or delays.

---

## Broader Cable Industry Stress and AI Routing Alternatives

Two additional risks operate at the level of the industry rather than the company. First, the broader cable sector faces structural pressure that extends well beyond the DOCSIS upgrade cycle. Overbuilder penetration, particularly from AT&T Fiber, has compressed subscriber counts at the largest MSOs, and the competitive response — price promotions, bundle discounts, accelerated infrastructure investment — has pressured free cash flow across the industry. A sustained cable sector capital cycle slowdown, driven by competitive attrition rather than technology strategy, would reduce addressable demand for CableOS regardless of its competitive position within that demand pool.

Second, and more speculatively but increasingly discussed among infrastructure analysts, the emergence of AI-driven data centre networking creates a substitution risk at the architectural level. As hyperscalers build private high-bandwidth networks optimised for AI workload traffic, and as edge computing architectures evolve, the traditional cable HFC network faces questions about its long-term role in a connectivity stack that increasingly routes traffic through radically different paths. This is a decade-horizon risk, not a near-term quarterly concern — but for a company whose equity valuation is substantially a function of long-duration growth expectations in cable broadband, the emergence of credible architectural alternatives is a factor that reprices those expectations at the margin, independent of any near-term execution outcome.

chapters.title: DOCSIS 4.0 transition, Video separation completion, AI routing optionality
chapters.body:
## The Pure-Play Pivot

By the frozen snapshot date in May 2026, the Video separation was completing the architectural simplification that the revenue trajectory had long implied. The revenue decline from $646 million (2022) to $580 million (2024) reflected Comcast deployment pacing, not structural deterioration — the platform model had been validated at a scale no competitor could yet match.

## DOCSIS 4.0: The Multi-Year Upgrade Cycle

The DOCSIS 4.0 migration — promising 10 Gbps downstream and symmetrical upstream via Extended Spectrum or Full Duplex architectures — is the demand thesis underpinning CableOS's trajectory. The virtualised architecture allows operators to upgrade through software rather than node-by-node replacement, a differentiation that anchored the Comcast relationship and supplies the proof-of-concept for broader operator conversations. Comcast and Charter have committed publicly to upgrade paths spanning 2025–2027 and beyond.

## Video Separation: Anatomy of a Divestiture

The $145 million MediaKind transaction (announced December 2025, closing expected Q2 2026) completes the disentanglement of two businesses that had shared infrastructure and salesforce for three decades. The post-separation Broadband entity carries a simpler equity story: a pure-play vCMTS company with Comcast as anchor, Charter as second major relationship, and a growing international pipeline.

## Revenue Profile of the Post-Separation Entity

The post-separation Broadband entity — built on $488 million FY2024 segment revenue — was expected to carry a materially different growth profile than the consolidated figure suggested. DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade contracts plus international operator wins are the forward demand levers for a management team no longer balancing video against broadband.

## AI Routing Optionality

CableOS's cloud-native architecture generates continuous telemetry on traffic volumes, congestion patterns, and spectrum utilisation — an input surface for AI-driven network optimisation (intelligent routing, predictive maintenance, dynamic spectrum allocation) that was not commercially developed through the frozen window but represents meaningful product-roadmap optionality. The architectural foundation means AI-layer capability additions require no new hardware at the operator level, an important commercial enabler as intelligent network management matures. [CableLabs](https://www.cablelabs.com) and principal operators were actively exploring this pathway.

## The 2026–2027 Positioning

As of the frozen snapshot, Harmonic's post-separation Broadband entity stood at the intersection of three converging dynamics: the cable industry's most technically demanding upgrade cycle in its history; a commercial anchor relationship providing both revenue stability and a reference platform; and a cloud-native architecture preserving AI-capability optionality. The company Ben-Natan leads into the second half of the decade is smaller, more focused, and anchored to a technology transition measured not in quarters but in five-to-seven-year infrastructure replacement cycles.
